messages.subject_clean: secr.test with certain models crashes R
messages.body_plain:
Hi Again!

I may have found a crash bug in secr.test (or perhaps in sim.secr called by secr.test); I am not sure exactly what the problem is (maybe a memory issue) but the trigger seems to be related to my model parameters.  Perhaps the “fix” is just another check and fail to error message to prevent the R crash, but I’m not really sure.

I’ve included the code to trigger the crash, along with an RDS file of my secr.fit outputs for 4 different models using the same multi-session capture data.  The first one runs fine with secr.test (albeit very slowly), I stopped it after the first “sim.secr fitting replicate 1…” message but I assume it would continue.  The fourth one triggers a crash in less than a minute before anything prints to the console.  The second and third secr.fit outputs I didn’t try running with secr.test, but are included in case the variations are helpful.

Thanks,

Scott

### secr.test crash example ###

library(secr)
library(dplyr)

SECR_S4_M4G1_SMAM_C245 <- readRDS("SECR_S4_M4G1_SMAM_C245.RDS")

### This one runs ###
secr.test_Test1 <- SECR_S4_M4G1_SMAM_C245 %>%
  filter(rn==1) %>%
  pull(results) %>%
  .[[1]] %>%
  secr.test(.,fit=TRUE)

### This one crashes R ###
secr.test_Test2 <- SECR_S4_M4G1_SMAM_C245 %>%
  filter(rn==4) %>%
  pull(results) %>%
  .[[1]] %>%
  secr.test(.,fit=TRUE)

messages.subject_clean: Seeking suggestions to reduce size of data
messages.body_plain:
Hi secr group,

I'm seeking suggestions on how I can further reduce the size of my data so secr models can run on my laptop. I have two years of data from a study where I collected fecal pellets from walking transects. There was a single occasion each year in a 3,797 square kilometer area.

Summary of the files I'm working with:
capture history file: two years of capture histories with 122 and 167 individuals detected. Sex information is included but ignored for now.
trap files: two trapfiles, one for each year with 974 and 870 points, respectively, from 2-km. transects segmented by 300 meters. Each file has three covariates.
telemetry file: subset of 300 total points from 17 females in the second year. Home range estimates from the subset are similar to the entire dataset. Sex is included but ignored for now.
Habitat mask: created with a buffer of 8 km. and 500-meter resolution in the study area boundary with non-habitat removed. 500 meters is the max resolution recommended given estimates of sigma. The mask has four covariates and is 131.6 MB.

I have all files and a secr script in a zipped folder (~11 MB) but it won't allow me to post a message when attached.

All files are scaled from meters to kilometers (divided by 1000) and covariates are centered and scaled. I can get two models to run: the null model and a model with session as a g0 covariate. When I include other covariates, I get errors like "Error in gethr... c,m,t combinations exceed 1e8 in gethr." and "cannot allocate vector of size 21.1 Gb." My laptop has 16 GB of RAM.

I would love to hear any suggestions or thoughts you have to accomplish my analysis.

Thank you,

Jennifer E. Nelson

messages.subject_clean: Adjusting for change in study area size necessary?
messages.body_plain:
Hi again.  I plan on using Murray's suggestion to use the open models to estimate lambda (my primary parameter of interest) and then use closed models to estimate D (and N).  Given that strategy, does it make sense to try to fit an open model with bk and h2 effects on lambda0 and sigma when those parameters mostly go toward estimating D, with estimates of lambda being pretty robust to biases in D?  I was considering testing some simpler models to estimate lambda (e.g., phi~t, lambda~t, lambda0~1, p~1) to decrease computing time and because the JSSA models are so finnicky when the become more complex.  Thanks!

On Wednesday, July 20, 2022 at 5:14:14 PM UTC-4 murray...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Joe
> Good to see you working on this dataset. When I looked at it a few years ago one of my hesitations was that I didn't have usage data for some spots that seemed not to have been sampled in some years (spillway 2007, 2011). Now you're onto it!
>
> Usage data alone will take care of the differences in sampling - no need for a covariate. I'm not quite sure what you mean by a Pradel model type.
>
> It's a puzzle how to estimate D (and N) when the extent of habitat changes between years because of flooding. My first reaction is that you could come really unstuck using an open model, because there are very specific unmodelled effects (limited temporary movement out of flooded areas, changing extent of habitat). If you are happy to argue/have good evidence that bears suirvive in situ then this is not an issue, and the open D-hat (N-hat) apply. I tend to place more trust in closed models for D (and N), anyway.
> Cheers
> Murray

I am using openCR to estimate D and N, recruitment, phi etc. using a Pradel-model type.  My question is whether I should use the number of traps each year as a covariate on overall detection or will this be accounted for automatically by the usage data?  Previous analyses suggest that the majority of bears do not shift their home ranges because of flooding so I would not expect a big increase in density in the areas that were not flooded during flood years.  How should I estimate N from D for those years?

Many thanks
Bryony

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bryony,

It might be one of these things:

1) the difference between expected and realised abundance. There is more info in the help on region.N but in essence the first is an expectation over many hypothetical animal populations (multiple realisations of the process that SCR assumes generates animal activity centres). There's no need for this to be larger than the number of animals that you detected, or were there, at the time of your survey. The second is an estimate of how many leopards there were at the time of the survey, and will always be bigger than the number of animals you detected.

2) with only 13 individuals fitting t and b models might be asking too much of the data, depending on numbers of recaptures. Maybe start with a null model and see if the pattern persists.

3) something went wrong in the conversion from density to abundance if you did this manually. You said density (number of animals per ha or km2) = 8.53 but treat it as an abundance (number of animals) in the comparison to 13. I guess you meant abundance all the way through though, but just putting here in case!

Hope that helps figure things out!

Ian

messages.subject_clean: secr.test with certain models crashes R
messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott
I think this was caused by a bug in sim.secr: it failed with learned-response models (b, B, bk etc.). For example,

library(secr)
test1 <- secr.test(secrdemo.b)
test2 <- secr.test(secrdemo.b)

crashed R at the second call of secr.test.

I've fixed this particular issue in the pre-release version (secr 4.5.8 2022-11-08) available as Windows binary <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_4.5.8.zip> or source <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_4.5.8.tar.gz> from the Density website. There may be more. Your model is certainly slow (I'd start with fit = FALSE).

A couple of other points. Remember the MLE of detection parameters (g0, lambda0) use a multi-catch model, and single-catch simulations with these estimates are likely to mislead. The piped commands add an unnecessary level of obscurity for many users, including me.

Murray

Ah! A chance for me to warn against interpreting the 'effective trapping area' as a geographic area. It isn't. Effective trapping area is a number calculated as an amalgam of detection parameters (e.g., g0, sigma), the distribution of detectors, and the duration of sampling. Technical details in Borchers & Efford 2008 <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/Borchers%20&%20Efford%20Biometrics%202008.pdf>. This clashes with informal pre-SECR concepts of effective trapping area (e.g. Otis et al. 1978).

messages.body_plain:
Further...

You mention 'g0' but that is not a parameter for detectfn = 14 (HHN).

Altogether you have a large mask (~15000 points), many detectors per
session (~900) and many levels of continuous covariates 'effort'
(~100) and 'precip' (~70).

There is no merit in keeping that many levels of the covariates - they
could easily be discretized. Better still, code effort in the 'usage'
attribute of traps - that can be continuous with no penalty, and
doesn't require fitting an extra parameter (once coded, can suppress
for a particular model fit with details = list(ignoreusage=TRUE)).

I found that splitting detectors into discrete sessions (32 clusters
for year 1, 34 for year 2) improved the fit time of the null model
from about 1000 seconds to 60 seconds. Each cluster then has its own
local mask of about 1000 points. I'll send some code offline.

Murray
